title: A close reading of word2vec: how words become vectors and why king - man + woman equals queen
summary: word2vec strips out the expensive hidden layer of neural network language models and uses CBOW and Skip-gram to learn word vectors from billions of words, making word meaning computable with addition and subtraction for the first time. We work through the model costs by hand, walk through the analogy task with a tiny 3D toy example, and then look at the errors hiding in the paper's own results.
ai_summary: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space (Google, 2013) introduces CBOW and Skip-gram, two log-linear models with no hidden layer. One predicts the middle word from its context, the other predicts context words from the middle word, so word vectors with hundreds of dimensions can be learned quickly from billions of words. The paper builds a test set of 8,869 semantic analogy questions and 10,675 syntactic ones, answered with vector arithmetic plus cosine similarity. A 300-dimensional Skip-gram model reaches 53.3% total accuracy, far above the previous best published word vectors' 24.6%; a 1,000-dimensional version trained on 6 billion words reaches 65.6%. The paper also argues that dimensionality and data should be scaled up together. Its limitation is that each word has a single context-independent vector.
brief: Problem: words are treated as isolated indices with no similarity between them; the neural network language models that can learn word vectors are too slow to use on very large data.
Method: remove the non-linear hidden layer and learn word vectors with CBOW (context predicts middle word) and Skip-gram (middle word predicts context), paired with hierarchical softmax.
Result: training cost drops by one to two orders of magnitude; Skip-gram leads by a wide margin on semantic analogy questions, and “king - man + woman ≈ queen” becomes the classic example.
Limitation: each word has only one context-independent vector; the model does not understand word morphology, and it learns co-occurrence associations rather than facts.

paper.title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space
paper.authors: Tomas Mikolov, Kai Chen, Greg Corrado, Jeffrey Dean

cover.headline: A close reading of the original word2vec paper
cover.highlight: Word meaning can be computed with addition and subtraction

blocks.p: In January 2013, four Google researchers — Tomas Mikolov, Kai Chen, Greg Corrado, and Jeff Dean — published this 12-page paper. It introduced two extremely simple models, **CBOW** and **Skip-gram**, for turning each word into a vector of a few hundred numbers. Together with the later open-sourced toolkit, they became known as **word2vec**.

Two things make it matter. The first is **speed**: by removing the hidden layer, the most expensive part of neural network language models at the time, the same computer can process far more data. The paper says high-quality word vectors can be learned from a 1.6 billion-word dataset in less than a day. The second is **quality**: the learned vectors contain regularities, the most famous being “king - man + woman ≈ queen.” Word meaning can be computed with arithmetic.

This is the first piece in our language-model learning track. From here on, a word is no longer an isolated index but a point in space; everything that follows — Seq2Seq, attention, Transformer, GPT — is built on that starting point. In today's large models, the first layer is still called the **embedding** layer, and it still does exactly this.

callout.title: The one-sentence version
callout.text: Represent each word as a vector in a few hundred dimensions so that words that appear in similar contexts end up close together in space. CBOW predicts the middle word from its surrounding words; Skip-gram predicts the surrounding words from the middle word. Without a hidden layer, the model is simple enough to train on billions of words, and the resulting vectors can answer analogy questions like “France is to Paris as Germany is to ?” by addition and subtraction.

callout.title: Three small concepts you'll need
callout.text: If you don't know them yet, these three are all you need:
list: **Vector**: an ordered list of numbers, such as (0.2, -1.3, 0.7). Two vectors can be added or subtracted, and you can compare whether they point in similar directions.
**Language model**: a model that predicts the next word from the preceding text. In 2013, the best language models were neural networks, but they were slow to train.
**Softmax**: turns a set of scores into probabilities that sum to 1. With a vocabulary of one million words, it has to compute one million scores — the main computational cost.

sections.h: The problem: to a computer, “cat” and “dog” are unrelated

blocks.p: Before word2vec, most NLP systems treated words as **atoms**: each word was just an index in a vocabulary — “cat” might be index 3051 and “dog” index 8722. The indices had no relationship to each other, so “cat” was as far from “dog” as it was from “democracy.”

The paper accepts that this approach has its reasons: it is simple and robust, and simple models trained on huge amounts of data often beat complex models trained on less data. The popular N-gram models of the time, for example, could already be trained on trillions of words. But in areas where high-quality data is limited, such as speech recognition and machine translation, simple methods have hit their limit: adding more data no longer brings clear improvement.

callout.title: Indices vs. coordinates
callout.text: Treating words as indices is like knowing only the postal code of each city: codes 100000 and 100001 being adjacent does not mean the cities are next to each other. Treating words as vectors is like giving each city a latitude and longitude: nearby cities have nearby coordinates, and you can compare the direction from Beijing to Tianjin with the direction from Shanghai to Suzhou. What word2vec aims to do is find a meaningful “coordinate” for every word.

blocks.p: The idea of giving words coordinates already existed, called **distributed representations**: a word is jointly represented by a few hundred numbers, each of which helps represent many words. The 2003 neural network language model by Bengio et al. learned word vectors as a byproduct of learning a language model. The problem was speed: the paper says that, to the authors' knowledge, no previous architecture had been successfully trained on more than a few hundred million words, and vector dimensionality was only 50 to 100.
So the paper's goal is explicit: **learn high-quality word vectors from billions of words and a vocabulary of millions, both quickly and well**.

sections.h: Why the old models were slow: counting the cost per training example

blocks.p: The paper first defines a common cost measure for all models: how many parameters are accessed during training. Total cost O = E × T × Q, where E is the number of training epochs, T is the number of words in the training set, and Q is the per-example cost, which depends on the model.

**Feedforward neural network language model (NNLM)** predicts the next word from the previous N words. It consists of input, projection, hidden, and output layers: at the input layer, each of the N words is looked up as a D-dimensional vector in the projection layer; these are fed into a non-linear hidden layer with H units; and finally the output layer produces a probability for each of the V words in the vocabulary. The per-example cost is:

formula.expr: Q = N × D + N × D × H + H × V

parts.desc: Looking up vectors for N words: cheap, just a table lookup
Projection-to-hidden connection: the projection layer is dense, so this term is expensive
Hidden-to-output connection: a score must be computed for every word in the vocabulary. When V is on the order of one million, this is the largest term.

formula.note: The expensive H × V term can be reduced to about H × log_{2}(V) with hierarchical softmax, explained below. Once it is reduced, the bottleneck becomes the middle term N × D × H — the non-linear hidden layer.

plain.title: Where the cost goes
plain.text: The per-example cost of old models has three parts. After hierarchical softmax, the last part is no longer expensive; almost all the time goes to the middle part: feeding the context through a large hidden layer (red bar). The word2vec idea is to cut exactly that part.

blocks.p: **Recurrent neural network language model (RNNLM)** does not need to fix the context at N previous words: the hidden layer connects back to itself, giving it a kind of short-term memory. Its per-example cost is Q = H × H + H × V, and with hierarchical softmax the bottleneck becomes the hidden layer's H × H term.

callout.title: Hierarchical softmax: replacing a one-in-a-million choice with twenty questions
callout.text: To choose one word out of a million, ordinary softmax has to score every word. Hierarchical softmax arranges the vocabulary into a binary tree; predicting a word becomes walking down from the root, answering a “left or right” question at each step. One million words need only about 20 questions (2^20 is roughly one million). The paper goes further by using a Huffman tree: frequent words are placed near the root, so they need fewer questions. The paper says that with a vocabulary of one million, this is about twice as fast as a balanced binary tree.

blocks.p: Both old models point to the same conclusion: **the non-linear hidden layer is the most expensive part.** It is exactly what makes neural networks powerful; but if the goal is only to learn word vectors, it may not be necessary.

sections.h: Two new models: CBOW and Skip-gram, no hidden layer

blocks.p: The paper's key decision: **accept a simpler, less expressive model so it can be trained on far more data.** Both new models have no hidden layer; only two steps remain — look up word vectors and classify the output. They are log-linear models.

fig.title: CBOW and Skip-gram: one predicts the middle from context, the other predicts context from the middle
fig.subtitle: Based on Section 3 and Figure 1 of the paper
rows: Four words before and after the middle word
Every word within a window before and after
Averages context word vectors (order ignored, hence “bag-of-words”)
Faster; slightly better on syntactic questions

plain.title: One predicts the middle, the other predicts its neighbors
plain.text: CBOW is like a cloze test: seeing “the cat on the mat,” guess the missing word in the middle, “sat.” Skip-gram is the reverse: seeing “sat,” guess which words might appear around it. Both training setups force the model to place words that often co-occur into similar positions.

blocks.p: **CBOW** (Continuous Bag-of-Words) is much like the feedforward language model with the hidden layer removed, with two differences: it looks at both past and future words, not just preceding words, and it averages the context word vectors directly, discarding word order. The paper found that using the four previous and four next words to predict the middle word works best.

**Skip-gram** is the reverse: it takes the middle word as input and predicts each word within a certain distance before and after it. Since more distant words are usually less related to the current word, the paper gives them less chance of being selected: with maximum distance C = 10, it randomly picks an R between 1 and C for each example, then predicts only the R words before and the R words after. Close words are therefore always predicted, while distant words are only occasional targets.
The paper does not state the training objective as a formula. Here is the standard form from the follow-up paper (Mikolov et al., NIPS 2013) to make clear what Skip-gram optimizes:

parts.desc: The input word (the middle word); v_{I} is its “input vector,” which is the final word vector we want.
A context word to be predicted; v'_{O} is its “output vector.”
The dot product of the two vectors: the more aligned their directions, the larger the value, and the more the model believes the words co-occur.
A sum over all V words in the vocabulary, used to turn scores into probabilities. This step is too expensive, hence hierarchical softmax.

formula.note: Training adjusts all vectors so that word pairs that really occur together get as high a probability as possible. The result: words that appear in similar contexts are pushed into similar directions.

callout.title: Why predicting neighbors learns word meaning
callout.text: Linguistics has an old saying: you can tell what a word means by the company it keeps. Around “cat” and “dog” you often find “feed,” “pet,” “fur”; to predict these words correctly, the model has no choice but to give the two similar vectors. Nobody tells the model that cats and dogs are both animals — it extracts that conclusion from billions of sentences on its own.

quiz.q: CBOW averages the context word vectors. What information does this discard?
quiz.why: Addition does not care about order: “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” average to exactly the same context vector, hence the name “bag of words.” Word meaning is exactly what the vectors store; the middle word is the prediction target; vocabulary size has nothing to do with this averaging.

sections.h: Working through the numbers: how much cheaper the new models are

blocks.p: Plug the paper's cost formulas into typical parameters and the gap becomes clear. The table below uses D = H = 500 and a vocabulary V of one million (log_{2}(V) ≈ 20), all with hierarchical softmax:

fig.title: After removing the hidden layer, the per-example training cost drops by one to two orders of magnitude
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: calculated for this article from the paper's equations 2, 4, and 5 with typical parameters; not paper data. Amber denotes CBOW.
columns: Using N = 10 (8 for CBOW), D = H = 500, C = 10
rows: N × D + N × D × H + H × log_{2}V
fig.note: In NNLM, the N × D × H term accounts for more than 99% of the cost. CBOW and Skip-gram cut exactly that term. Skip-gram performs one classification per context word, so it costs about 7 times as much as CBOW.

blocks.p: Being one to two orders of magnitude cheaper means the same compute can train on far more data and use much higher dimensions. The paper's later experiments show this is exactly where the quality gains come from.

quiz.q: According to the paper's cost formula, where does most computation go in NNLM after applying hierarchical softmax?
options: Looking up word vectors, N × D
Projection to the non-linear hidden layer, N × D × H
All three are about the same
quiz.why: Plug in typical values: N × D × H is 2.5 million, while the other two terms together are only 15,000. That is why the paper targets the hidden layer: remove it, and the cost drops. Hierarchical softmax has already reduced the output layer from H × V to H × log_{2}V.

sections.h: How word vectors are tested: analogy questions with addition and subtraction

blocks.p: Before this, word vectors were often evaluated by listing a few words and their nearest neighbors, then judging by intuition whether they looked reasonable. The paper designs a stricter test: **analogy questions**. For example, “big is to biggest as small is to ?”

The answer comes purely from vector arithmetic: compute X = vector(“biggest”) − vector(“big”) + vector(“small”), then find the word in the vocabulary whose angle with X is smallest (highest cosine similarity), excluding the question words. If the result is exactly “smallest,” the answer is correct.

callout.title: Cosine similarity: direction, not length
callout.text: The cosine similarity of two vectors is the cosine of their angle: 1 for exactly the same direction, 0 for perpendicular, and -1 for opposite directions. It is used because a word vector's length often reflects word frequency, while its direction is closer to word meaning.

fig.title: A 3D toy example: king - man + woman lands closest to queen
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: vectors are invented for this article, with only 3 dimensions, each carrying meaning. Real word vectors have hundreds of dimensions, and any single dimension usually has no obvious meaning.
fig.note: “king - man” removes “male” and some of the “person” component, leaving “royalty”; adding “woman” restores the female part. In a real model, this gender direction is not a dimension specified in advance — it is a direction that emerges during training. By the rules, king, man, and woman are all excluded as question words, so the answer is queen.

plain.title: A parallelogram
plain.text: The step from “man” to “king” (green) is almost the same as the step from “woman” to “queen”: both are “adding royalty.” So starting from king, subtracting man and adding woman lands near queen. Differences in meaning become directions that can be translated through space.

blocks.p: The paper's test set has two broad categories: **semantic** questions, 8,869 of them, covering capital-to-country, currencies, city-to-state, and man-woman pairs; and **syntactic** questions, 10,675 of them, covering adjective-to-adverb, opposites, comparatives, superlatives, present participles, past tense, and noun plurals. For each category, a list of word pairs is first created by hand, then pairs are combined into questions; for example, 68 large US cities and their states yield about 2,500 questions.

Scoring is very strict: the found word must match **exactly** to count as correct; synonyms are marked wrong. The paper says 100% accuracy is therefore almost impossible, because the model has no knowledge of word morphology (such as the -ly and -est suffixes).

quiz.q: The paper requires an analogy answer to be exactly correct before it is counted. How does that affect scoring?
options: It deflates the scores: a synonym, or a word that is right in meaning but different in form, is marked wrong.
quiz.why: Strict matching is a conservative way to score; the model actually “understands” more than the number suggests. The paper later notes that, by this standard, the example table it shows scores only about 60%, but many of the “wrong” answers are in fact quite close.

sections.h: Outcome 1: dimensionality and data must grow together

blocks.p: The paper trains on the Google News corpus, about 6 billion tokens in total, with the vocabulary limited to the 1 million most frequent words. It first runs a set of small CBOW experiments across different data sizes and dimensions (using only questions involving the 30,000 most frequent words):

fig.title: Raising dimensions alone or data alone brings diminishing returns; only raising both together keeps accuracy climbing
fig.subtitle: Unit: %, CBOW accuracy on a subset of analogy questions from Table 2 of the paper. Shading is illustrative; darker means higher accuracy.
fig.note: Look at the 50-dimension row: as data grows from 24 million to 783 million words, accuracy only rises from 13.4 to 23.2 — the dimension is too low to hold more information. Now look at the leftmost column: as dimensions grow from 50 to 600, accuracy only rises from 13.4 to 24.0 — there is too little data to learn more. Only when both grow together does accuracy reach 50.4.

plain.title: A bigger bucket needs a bigger pipe
plain.text: Vector dimensionality is like the size of a bucket; training data is like the pipe that fills it. If you only get a bigger bucket and keep the same pipe, the bucket never fills. If you only widen the pipe but keep a small bucket, the water overflows. Only when both grow together does accuracy keep climbing.

blocks.p: The conclusion sounds obvious, but the paper makes the point explicitly: at the time it was common to train 50- to 100-dimensional word vectors on very large data, and those dimensions are plainly too small. By CBOW's cost formula, doubling the data and doubling the dimensions add about the same amount of computation, so the two should be increased together. This is the same kind of question the scaling-laws work would take up seven years later: how model size and data should grow in tandem.

sections.h: Outcome 2: Skip-gram leads by a wide margin on semantic questions

blocks.p: To compare the four architectures fairly, the paper trains 640-dimensional vectors on the same data, about 320 million words with an 82,000-word vocabulary:

fig.title: Same data, same dimensionality: Skip-gram's semantic accuracy is more than double that of the other models
fig.subtitle: Unit: %, from Table 3 of the paper. Blue columns are semantic questions.
fig.note: The RNNLM vectors had previously been trained on a single CPU for about 8 weeks. RNNLM's word vectors are directly tied to its non-linear hidden layer, which the paper believes is why it underperforms on semantic questions.

blocks.p: The four architectures have different strengths: RNN vectors are mainly good on syntactic questions; NNLM is clearly better than RNN; CBOW beats NNLM on syntactic questions and is comparable on semantic ones; **Skip-gram is slightly behind CBOW on syntactic questions but far ahead of every model on semantic ones.**

Compared with the published word vectors available at the time (Table 4), the gap is even clearer: the previous best published total accuracy was only 24.6% (Mikolov's own 640-dimensional RNNLM vectors), while a 300-dimensional Skip-gram trained on 783 million words reaches 53.3%, and CBOW reaches 36.1%. On a single CPU, CBOW trained for about a day, Skip-gram for about three days.

**One pass beats three.** The paper also finds that doubling the data and training for a single epoch works about as well as, or better than, training for three epochs on the original data—and it is faster. For example, a single-pass Skip-gram over 1.6 billion words scores 53.8% total, slightly above the 53.3% from three passes over 783 million words.

fig.title: At scale: 1,000-dimensional vectors from 6 billion words in about two days
fig.subtitle: From Table 6 of the paper, trained using the DistBelief distributed framework. Training time is shown as days × CPU cores; core counts are estimates. Amber denotes Skip-gram.
fig.note: The paper says the 1,000-dimensional NNLM would have taken too long to train and was not completed. Measured as days × cores, the new models used only about one eighth to one ninth as much computation as the NNLM while producing vectors with 10 times the dimensionality and higher accuracy.

quiz.q: Why does Skip-gram do markedly better than CBOW on semantic questions? Which of these explanations is the most plausible?
options: Skip-gram makes a separate prediction for each context word, so each word receives more, finer-grained training signal instead of being averaged away.
Skip-gram is trained on more data.
quiz.why: The paper itself gives no reason; this is a common explanation. CBOW averages the context into a single vector before predicting the middle word, so rare-word information is easily averaged away; Skip-gram has each word predict each of its neighbors separately, producing a richer training signal. In the comparison, the two models had the same dimensionality and training data, and neither had a hidden layer.

sections.h: What was learned: elegant regularities and clear errors

blocks.p: The paper uses the best Skip-gram vectors from Table 4 (300 dimensions, trained on 783 million words) to show a batch of analogy results. As you read the table, try spotting the errors yourself:

fig.title: The analogies shown in the paper: mostly correct, with quite a few clear mistakes
fig.subtitle: From Table 8 of the paper. Each row uses the relationship from the leftmost pair to infer the remaining examples. Parentheses mark errors or questionable answers added by this site; the amber row gets two of its three examples wrong.
rows: Mozart : violinist (questionable: composer would fit better)
fig.note: The full table has 10 rows; six are shown here. The paper itself says that under strict-match scoring, the table earns only about 60%.

blocks.p: These mistakes are instructive. The vectors learn who tends to appear with whom, so next to IBM it is easy to find the CEO of Sun, and France and Spanish tapas appear in the same kinds of articles. The model learns **associations**, not **facts**.

The paper also mentions two other uses. Averaging the vectors of 10 examples instead of using a single example to represent a relationship improves accuracy on the semantic and syntactic questions by about 10 percentage points. Averaging a group of words, then finding the word farthest away from that average, can solve odd-one-out puzzles.

On Microsoft's sentence completion challenge (1,040 sentences, each missing one word with five choices), Skip-gram alone scores only 48.0%, below LSA's 49%; combined with an RNN language model in a weighted combination, it reaches 58.9%, above the previous best of 55.4%. Word vectors and language models capture complementary information.

list: **One word, one vector**: “apple” gets the same vector whether it means the fruit or the company; the river-bank and financial-bank senses of “bank” are mixed together. The word vector itself has no notion of context.

**No knowledge of word structure**: the model treats big, bigger, and biggest as three unrelated words and learns them separately, ignoring the regularity of the endings. The paper notes that adding information about word structure could further improve the syntactic scores.
**Word order is lost**: CBOW directly averages the context, and Skip-gram only predicts neighbors one by one. Neither pays attention to sentence structure.

**Limited evaluation**: analogy questions test the linear structure of the vectors, and the paper only “believes” that this metric is positively correlated with real-world usefulness. It was not validated across a broad range of downstream tasks.

blocks.p: **A few small discrepancies in the paper.** The abstract says high-quality vectors can be learned from a 1.6 billion-word dataset “in less than a day.” According to Table 5, that is true for CBOW (0.6 days for one epoch), but Skip-gram on the same data takes 2 days. Also, the two models are usually called word2vec, but that name never appears in the body of this paper; it comes from the authors' later open-source code.

**What happened next.** The paper's last section notes that the authors later released an open-source, single-machine multithreaded C++ implementation that processes billions of words per hour, plus more than 1.4 million named-entity vectors trained on over 100 billion words. Their NIPS paper in the same year (Mikolov et al., 2013) added **negative sampling** (comparing against only a few randomly chosen “negative” examples instead of a full softmax) and **subsampling of frequent words**—that is what most people today mean by word2vec.

As we continue along the learning track, the next questions arise naturally: what if a word's meaning depends on its context? What if we need to process not a single word but a whole sentence and translate it into another sentence? That is the problem Seq2Seq (2014) will take up. Later, ELMo, BERT, and GPT all give each word a **context-dependent** vector, but their first layer is still a word2vec-style embedding table.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you really understand it?

quiz.q: During Skip-gram training, maximum distance C = 10, and each example randomly draws R from 1 to 10, predicting only R words before and after. What is the effect of this?
options: It makes training more random and prevents overfitting.
Nearby words are predicted almost every time, while distant words are only occasional—effectively giving nearby words more weight.
It makes the computation per example fixed.
It makes rare words appear more often.
quiz.why: A neighbor at distance 1 is predicted for any R; a neighbor at distance 10 is predicted only when R happens to be 10, so one time in ten. The paper's reasoning is that distant words are usually less related to the current word, so they should be sampled less.

quiz.q: What word is “France - Paris + Tokyo” most likely to produce, and what kind of relationship does the question test?
quiz.why: “France - Paris” gives the country-minus-capital direction; adding Tokyo lands near Japan. Capital and country are in the paper's semantic category; comparatives and plurals are syntactic. Tokyo itself is one of the question words, so it is excluded.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: What is the essential difference between treating words as indices and treating them as vectors?
Why were the old neural network language models slow? Where was the bulk of the cost?
How does hierarchical softmax turn a one-in-a-million choice into twenty yes/no questions? What extra speed does a Huffman tree provide?
What does CBOW predict and from what? What does Skip-gram predict and from what? Which kind of question is each better at?
Why does predicting neighbors push similar words into similar vectors?
How are analogy questions answered with vector addition/subtraction and cosine similarity? Why does strict matching underrate the model?
Why do dimensionality and data need to increase together?
What problems come from having one vector per word? How do later models address them?
